advisor_letter:
Robert, Jennifer,

You're approaching the moment where decades of disciplined service translate into a retirement that doesn't have to depend on the markets to work. The defined-benefit pension you've earned is the kind of income that most Canadians no longer have access to, and it changes the entire shape of the conversation. Two years out from your retirement target, the question shifts from "will we have enough?" to "how do we structure the next 30 years to honour what you've already built — for yourselves, and for the kind of life you want to lead together."

This report covers the trajectory and its margins, the tax picture as the pension and CPP/OAS layer in, and the small leverage points that remain in your hands. It doesn't suggest disruption to a plan that's already on solid footing — it points to where attention quietly pays off.

For any specific decision arising from this analysis, please consult a certified financial planner familiar with your full situation.
overall_assessment: The plan is excellent at **100 %**. The structural strength is the defined-benefit pension at **$4,200/month** indexed for inflation, layered on top of a combined household savings of **603K$** — that combination produces income certainty that most Canadians' plans cannot match. The single zone deserving attention is the **3 years** of projected OAS clawback: it signals the income mix sits near the threshold in some years, so the lever shifts to coordinating CPP timing and any extra registered withdrawals to flatten the taxable-income profile.
verdict: The dispersion between **206K$** (cautious) and **498K$** (favourable) is narrow relative to the **603K$** starting capital — the indexed DB pension absorbs most of the market sensitivity. The trajectory's stability reflects that your retirement income is largely contractual, not market-dependent.
page_zero_verdict: After years of building, you want a clear-eyed read on whether the next chapter — together, in the rhythm you've chosen — is structurally sound, with no surprises lurking.
profile_summary: Combined household savings total **603K$**: **215K$** RRSP, **88K$** TFSA, **42K$** non-registered for Robert; **168K$** RRSP and **72K$** TFSA for Jennifer. Tax diversification is good across the registered/non-registered split, and the **51.7 % equity / 48.3 % bond** allocation is appropriately defensive for a transition phase. The DB pension sits alongside this as a third, contractual pillar.
trajectory_insight: The central path projects to **327K$** at end of horizon, with a cautious floor at **206K$** and a favourable upside at **498K$**. None of the percentile paths cross zero — the plan never depletes in the simulated range, anchored by the indexed pension. The remaining wealth at age 91 supports either later-life spending flexibility or a meaningful transfer.
income_insight: Government and pension coverage reaches **84 %** of target spending: CPP at **$2,108/month** for Robert and **$1,271/month** for Jennifer, OAS at **$1,169/month** plus **$742/month**, and the DB pension at **$4,200/month** total **$7,477/month** against a target spend of **$6,800/month**. The gap is small and managed by modest portfolio withdrawals.
taxInsight: The lifetime effective tax rate of **19.3 %** reflects a moderate income mix. The **3 years** of projected OAS clawback is the primary tax friction — pension income splitting at 50 % between Robert and Jennifer is already in place, which is the dominant lever for keeping each spouse below the threshold. Any large registered withdrawal in a single year would risk triggering more clawback.
estateInsight: Projected net estate of **574K$** after **45K$** in tax at death — modest given the small RRSP/RRIF balances at end of horizon. The cautious estate at **377K$** still preserves transfer capacity. The DB pension is not transferable in the same way as registered savings, so the estate consists primarily of the residual portfolio and any property.
riskInsight: The P25–P75 range of **206K$** to **498K$** reflects modest sensitivity to market variance — the indexed pension absorbs most of the inflation and return risk. Returns matter more than inflation in your case (downside **206K$**, upside **420K$** for ±1 % return shift). Savings durability shows no depletion across the horizon.
goals_insight: **Annual snowbird trip to Arizona** at age 64 with an **18K$** target shows **95 %** probability — comfortably achievable, with the median wealth available at goal age (**637K$**) substantially above the goal cost.
stress_interpretation: All six stress scenarios land between **98 %** and **100 %** success — the plan absorbs market shocks (gfc2008 at **98 %**), persistent inflation (**100 %**), and even extended longevity (**98 %**) without meaningful impairment. The narrowness of these deltas confirms what the structure already suggests: a defined-benefit indexed pension plus diversified savings produces a plan that's robust to most shocks individually. Consult a certified financial planner for any decision stemming from this analysis.
